entries.modern_form: PIE *h₂éḱru 'tear' (Indo-Iranian/Baltic/Tocharian) beside PIE *dáḱru 'tear' (Greek, Italic, Celtic, Germanic, Armenian)
entries.note: Both reconstructions are real and both glosses are right, but Pokorny prints them as TWO separate lemmas — 'akru ‚Träne‘' on p.23 and 'dakrú n. ‚Träne‘' on p.179 — and says explicitly of the pair: 'Das Verhältnis zu idg. *dakru ‚Träne‘ ist ungeklärt' (POK_01.txt \f-page 31, printed p.23) and, under dakru, 'Andrerseits sucht man Vermittlung mit ai. áśru ... wohl bloßes Reimwort ... s. oben S. 23 unter akru' (\f-page 187 area, printed p.179). Nourai's single box 'Akru, Dakru' therefore states as settled what Pokorny leaves open. He is not alone: Buck 16.38 lists 'IE *dakru-, also *draku- and *aḱru-, relations variously explained', and Aryanpur (ARY, printed p.90) puts Av. asrū-, Skt. áśru, Gk. dákru, Lat. lacrima and Eng. tear in one family. Modern Wiktionary keeps the two apart and calls the link 'uncertain', citing Dunkel's *d (zero grade of *ád) prefixed to *h₂éḱru, or a compound *dr̥ḱ-h₂éḱru 'eye-bitter'. Verdict 'plausible' rather than 'confirmed' only because of the merge; every individual word in the chart belongs to one branch or the other. Note also that the two halves of the chart are consistent: the Iranian/Persian branch hangs off *akru, the Germanic/English branch off *dakru.
entries.note_fa: هر دو بازسازی اصیل‌اند و معنای هر دو نیز درست است، اما پوکورنی آن‌ها را دو مدخل جداگانه می‌آورد: «akru اشک» در ص ۲۳ و «dakrú اشک» در ص ۱۷۹، و دربارهٔ نسبت این دو صریحاً می‌نویسد «رابطهٔ آن با *dakru هندواروپایی روشن نیست». پس نورایی با گنجاندن هر دو در یک خانه، چیزی را قطعی نموده است که پوکورنی آن را گشوده نهاده بود. البته او در این کار تنها نیست: باک نیز «*dakru- و نیز *draku- و *aḱru-» را با یادداشت «نسبتشان به وجوه گوناگون تبیین شده» می‌آورد و آریان‌پور نیز اوستایی asrū-، سنسکریت áśru، یونانی dákru، لاتین lacrima و انگلیسی tear را در یک خانواده می‌نشاند؛ اما ویکی‌واژه دو ریشه را جدا نگاه می‌دارد و پیوندشان را «نامسلّم» می‌خواند و از دو تبیین یاد می‌کند: پیشوند *d (به تحلیل دونکل) یا ترکیب *dr̥ḱ-h₂éḱru «تلخیِ چشم». حکم «با احتیاط پذیرفتنی» تنها به سبب همین ادغام است، وگرنه تک‌تک واژه‌های نمودار به یکی از دو شاخه تعلق دارند و دو نیمهٔ نمودار نیز با خود سازگارند: شاخهٔ ایرانی از *akru و شاخهٔ ژرمنی از *dakru آویخته است.

nodes.derivation: Avestan asrū- n. 'tear' is genuine and well attested — Bartholomae, AiW s.v. (BRT.txt line 5925): "'asrū- n. 'Träne'; ai. āśrav-, np. ars" — and appears in the compound asrū.azan- 'shedding tears' (Yt. 10.38). It continues Proto-Iranian *Hácru < PIE *h₂éḱru, with Indo-Iranian *ć > Iranian s before the following r. The SECOND form, 'asraka', is not an attested Avestan word: it is Horn's starred reconstruction, coined to explain NP ašk — Horn, Grundriss no. 88 (HRN.txt printed p.21): 'ešk ‚Thräne‘ ... aw. *asraka (vergl. skr. áśra-), *arsaka (Horn, Indog. Forsch. II, 136).' Hübschmann rejects it (see node #3). So the node is right for asrū-, over-stated for asraka.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian ars 'tear', written <ʾLS> in Book Pahlavi and <ʾrs> in Manichaean script, is the regular reflex of Old Iranian *asru-: the Iranian cluster -sr- metathesises to -rs- in Middle/New Persian (Hübschmann, Pers. Stud. p.171/p.220: 'ap. sr = np. rs: ars ‚Thräne‘ = zd. asru-'), and the final -u of the u-stem is lost. It is attested in the Bundahišn (Mo'in cites Bd. 90) and in the texts glossed by Nyberg (93¹⁷).

nodes.derivation: NP ars «ارس» (now archaic/poetic) is the direct continuation of MP ars, itself < Av. asrū- < PIr *Hácru < PIE *h₂éḱru; Borhan-e Qate' p.103 defines it «و بفتح اول و سکون ثانی، اشک چشم را گویند» ('with a on the first and sukun on the second it means the tear of the eye'). The ordinary modern word ašk «اشک» is a DOUBLET, not a straight descendant of ars: it goes back to a k-suffixed *Hácru-ka- (Khotanese āṣka-, Wakhi yašk point the same way) and may have entered Persian from Parthian ʾšk /ašk/ rather than developing inside the south-western dialect, where *-sr- gave -rs-. Horn (no. 88) derived it from a reconstructed Av. *asraka; Hübschmann §88 explicitly objects: 'Da zd. asru- = skr. áśru- im Np. als ars (aus *asr) vorliegt, ist es nicht wahrscheinlich, dass ein zd. *asraka-, dem lautgesetzlich np. *asra entspräche, durch np. ašk vertreten wird', proposing instead as-k beside ars on the model of xʷas beside xusrū 'mother-in-law'. So the arrow Pahlavi ars → NP ašk is too simple, though both words are certainly from the same root.
nodes.derivation_fa: «ارس» فارسی نو (که امروز کهنه و شعری است) دنبالهٔ مستقیم ars فارسی میانه است، و آن از asrū- اوستایی و در نهایت از *h₂éḱru؛ برهان قاطع (ص ۱۰۳) آن را «اشک چشم» معنی کرده است. اما واژهٔ رایج امروزی، «اشک»، دوگانه (doublet) است نه دنبالهٔ مستقیم «ارس»: به *Hácru-ka- با پسوند k بازمی‌گردد (ختنی āṣka- و وخی yašk نیز همین را می‌نمایانند) و چه‌بسا از پارتی (ʾšk) به فارسی رسیده باشد، نه از گویش جنوب غربی که در آن *-sr- به -rs- بدل می‌شد. هرن (شمارهٔ ۸۸) آن را از *asraka اوستاییِ بازسازی‌شده می‌گرفت، اما هوبشمان صریحاً اعتراض می‌کند که «چون asru- اوستایی در فارسی نو به‌صورت ars آمده است، بعید است *asraka که به‌قاعده باید *asra بدهد در «اشک» بازتاب یافته باشد» و به‌جای آن as-k را در کنار ars می‌نهد، بر قیاس «خواس» در کنار «خسرو». پس پیکان ars پهلوی ← «اشک» فارسی ساده‌انگارانه است، هرچند هر دو واژه بی‌گمان از یک ریشه‌اند.

nodes.derivation: Proto-Germanic *tahrą (beside *tagrą) 'tear' is the regular Germanic outcome of PIE *dáḱru: Grimm's law turns *d- into *t- and the palatal *ḱ into *h (before the *-r- also *g by Verner/analogy), whence Gothic tagr, Old Norse tár, OHG zahar (NHG Zähre), OE tēar/teagor. Nourai's 'tahr' is Watkins's *tahr- exactly.

nodes.derivation: OE tēar (a contraction of the older teagor, itself < PGmc *tagrą) > ME tere, ter > NE tear (the noun, 'tear 1' as against the homograph 'tear 2' = to rend, from an unrelated PIE *der- 'flay'). No borrowing is involved; the word is inherited straight down the Germanic line from *tahr-/*tagr-.

entries.note: The root box is right; the trouble on this page is the EAGLE branch. Nourai hangs Av. 'arva' → Pahl. āluh → NP āleh, and Lat. 'aqualius' → Fr. aigle → Eng. eagle, on *akʷā- 'water'. Two independent problems: (a) 'arva' is not Avestan at all — it is the Pāzand/Middle-Persian form arvā of Bundahišn 14:23, which Mo'in cites in his own footnote at BQT p.58 and which Horn no. 43 quotes as 'arvā (Bund.) in Zendbuchstaben'; Bartholomae's AiW has no such word, Avestan for 'eagle' being ərəzifya- or saēna-. Nyberg derives Pahl. āluh from OP *ardūfya- < *ardifya- = Av. ərəzifya-, and Wiktionary from PIr *Hr̥jifyáh < PIE *h₂rǵ-i-pt-ió-s 'white/swift-flying' — i.e. the Iranian eagle-word has nothing to do with 'water'. (b) The Latin word is not 'aqualius' (no such Latin form exists); it is aquila 'eagle', fem. of aquilus 'dark-coloured'. The step aquilus < aqua is a Roman folk etymology reported by Festus ('aquilus autem color est ab aqua nominatus') and is rejected by Ernout-Meillet, LAT s.v. aquilus: 'L'explication par aqua rend mal compte du sens de l'adjectif; on ne voit pas pourquoi l'eau aurait été prise pour désigner une couleur tirant sur le noir'; de Vaan and Etymonline likewise call it uncertain. Pokorny p.23 does report it ('davon aquilus ‚dunkel‘, aquila ‚Adler‘, eigentl. ‚der Dunkelfarbige‘'), which is presumably where Nourai took it from, so the branch is old-fashioned rather than invented. Aryanpur (ARY p.68) records the same split: 'PARTRIDGE holds this word may be cognate with Latin AQUA (water)', while 'ONIONS and SKEAT go back only to the Latin root AQUILA' and Pokorny takes the Iranian, Armenian and Greek words from *er-/*or- 'eagle, large bird'. The water branches proper (Latin aqua, French eau/eau de Cologne, English aquarium/aquatic, Germanic *ahwjō → island) are all sound.

nodes.derivation: Latin aqua 'water' is the standard Italic reflex of PIE *h₂ékʷeh₂, cognate with Gothic aƕa 'river', OE ēa, OHG aha, and (probably) the Lusitanian river-word aqua. The root is 'suspiciously limited to a few western Indo-European branches' (Wiktionary), and Ernout-Meillet stress that it named water as an active, divine being rather than water as a substance (that is *wódr̥, Lat. unda).

nodes.derivation: Two things go wrong here. (i) The language label: arvā is not Avestan. It is a Pāzand form written in Avestan characters in the Middle-Persian Bundahišn — Horn no. 43 (HRN.txt printed p.10): 'āluh ‚Adler‘. phlv. āluh (Kārn. 59, Note 2), vergl. arvā (Bund.) in Zendbuchstaben'; Mo'in says the same at BQT p.58: «و نیز در بندهش (۱۴:۲۳) arvâ بمعنی عقاب آمده». Bartholomae's Altiranisches Wörterbuch has no arva-; the real Avestan words for 'eagle' are ərəzifya- (col. 354) and saēna-. (ii) The edge: as drawn the node descends from Latin aqua, which is impossible in both direction and family — an Iranian word cannot come out of Latin, and even as a shorthand for 'same root as' the connection fails, since Pahl. āluh/arvā goes back to PIr *Hr̥jifyáh < PIE *h₂rǵ-i-pt-ió-s (from *h₂erǵ- 'white, glittering', cf. Skt. r̥jipyá-, Gk. αἰγυπιός), not to *h₂ékʷeh₂ 'water'. Nourai's own NOTE concedes that his source VFO 'does not provide any derivation'.

nodes.derivation: The word itself is impeccable: Middle Persian āluh <ʾlwh>, Manichaean <ʾlwf>, 'eagle', attested in the Kārnāmag ī Ardašīr ī Pābagān 14:12 and in the Bundahišn (as Pāzand arvā). What is wrong is the parentage. Nyberg derives it 'MPrs ʾawf (List 79); NP āluh, < OP *ardūfya- < *ardifya-, Av. ərəzifya-' — that is, from Old Iranian *r̥difya- 'eagle' with the regular Middle Persian development *rd > l and loss of the palatal glide, giving āluh; Wiktionary's PIr *Hr̥jifyáh is the same reconstruction. Descent from Latin aqua via an 'Avestan arva' (as the chart draws it) has no support anywhere; Hübschmann §43 says only 'die Bildung von phl. np. āluh ist dunkel'.

nodes.derivation: There is no Latin word 'aqualius'. What Nourai means — his own gloss 'water (dark) colored bird, eagle' is a paraphrase of Klein's wording — is aquila 'eagle', explained by the Romans as the feminine of aquilus 'dark-coloured', itself supposedly 'water-coloured' from aqua. Klein (KLN:97, s.v. aquiline) states it in just those terms: 'L. aquilinus ... fr. aquila, ‚eagle‘, prob. lit. ‚the dark-colored (bird)‘, fem. of aquilus, ‚dark-colored‘, prop. ‚water-colored‘, fr. aqua, ‚water‘'; Funk & Wagnalls (FSD:779) has '< F. aigle, < L. aquila, orig. f. of aquilus, dark-colored'. But the aqua-etymology goes back to Festus ('aquilus autem color est ab aqua nominatus') and modern Latinists reject it: Ernout-Meillet, s.v. aquilus, 'L'explication par aqua rend mal compte du sens de l'adjectif; on ne voit pas pourquoi l'eau aurait été prise pour désigner une couleur tirant sur le noir', and s.v. aquila, 'le nom de l'aigle ... varie d'une langue indo-européenne à l'autre et résulte partout d'arrangements relativement récents'. De Vaan reverses the direction (aquilus 'dark' may itself be from aquila). Disputed both for the impossible form and for the aqua > aquilus step.

nodes.derivation: eau is the regular French descendant of Latin aqua: aqua > Vulgar Latin *awa > Old French ewe/eve (11th c.) > eaue > eau, the modern spelling fossilising a diphthongisation that is no longer pronounced ([o]). eau de Cologne, coined at Cologne in 1709 by Giovanni Maria Farina, is literally 'water of Cologne', the city name going back to Colonia (Agrippina). But 'aquarium' is NOT a French word inherited from aqua: Klein files it as 'L. aquarium, neut. of the adjective aquarius, ‚pertaining to water‘, used as a noun', and the modern sense was coined in English in 1830 (P. H. Gosse's 1854 book The Aquarium popularised it); French acquired aquarium as a learned borrowing of the same Latin word. Hence 'plausible': two of the three words are exactly right, the third is misfiled as French.
